questions.title: Recurrent hematuria with atypical urine cells and an ulcerated bladder mass indicates carcinoma
questions.question: A 62 years male patient has hematuria for many times in past week. Cytological examination of the urine showed atypical cells. Cystoscopy showed 5 cm ulcerated mass. Which of the following is best describe the lesion
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with recurrent hematuria; urine cytology shows atypical cells and cystoscopy shows a 5 cm ulcerated bladder mass.

explanations.A: Correct. An ulcerated, infiltrating bladder mass causing recurrent hematuria with atypical (malignant-appearing) cells on urine cytology is the classic clinical and cytological picture of a malignant epithelial tumour -- carcinoma, most commonly transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder in this age group. The ulceration itself, a feature of unrestrained invasive growth destroying the overlying epithelium, points to malignancy rather than a benign process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal, not epithelial, tumour; the urothelial lining atypia on cytology points to an epithelial-cell process.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adenoma is a benign glandular epithelial tumour; it would not typically present as an ulcerated infiltrating mass with atypical cells on cytology, features that indicate malignant behaviour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Papilloma is a benign tumour of non-glandular (transitional/urothelial) epithelium; a benign papilloma does not ulcerate or shed atypical malignant cells the way this lesion does.

questions.subtopic: Clinical recognition of carcinoma from hematuria and cytology
questions.learning_objective: Recognise a bladder carcinoma from recurrent hematuria, atypical urine cytology and an ulcerated cystoscopic mass.

questions.title: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of glands
questions.question: Adenocarcinoma is a:

explanations.A: Correct. Adenocarcinoma is the malignant tumour of glandular epithelium -- the malignant counterpart of adenoma. It shows the invasive, destructive growth and cytological atypia of a malignant tumour while still forming (to varying degrees) gland-like or duct-like structures reflecting its glandular origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of tissue elements normal to the site, not a true malignant neoplasm at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A benign tumour of glands is called an adenoma, not adenocarcinoma; the '-carcinoma' suffix specifically denotes malignant behaviour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A benign tumour of surface (non-glandular) epithelium is a papilloma; adenocarcinoma is both malignant and of glandular, not surface, origin.

questions.learning_objective: Define adenocarcinoma as the malignant tumour of glandular epithelium.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Malignant tumors of glands"

questions.title: Grade I, stage I designations mean well-differentiated and localized
questions.question: Review of a series of surgical pathology reports indicates that a certain type of neoplasm is diagnosed as grade I on a scale of I to IV. Clinically, some of the patients with this neoplasm are found to have stage I disease. Which of the following is the best interpretation of a neoplasm with these designations?
questions.vignette: Surgical pathology reports grade a neoplasm as grade I (of IV) and, clinically, some patients have stage I disease.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Grade and stage are both applied to already-diagnosed malignant neoplasms; they describe how malignant it is (grade) and how far it has spread (stage), not whether it is malignant at all.
explanations.B: Correct. Histological grade (I of IV) reflects how closely the tumour cells resemble their tissue of origin -- grade I means well-differentiated, closely resembling normal tissue and generally slower-growing. Clinical stage (I) reflects the anatomical extent of spread -- stage I means the tumour is localized, without regional or distant spread. Together, grade I and stage I describe a well-differentiated, localized neoplasm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Grade and stage say nothing about the specific tissue of origin (epithelial versus mesenchymal); a tumour of either lineage can be graded and staged this way.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An in situ component (confined within the basement membrane, not yet invasive) is a distinct histological finding, not what grade I / stage I designations specifically indicate.

questions.subtopic: Interpreting tumour grade and stage together
questions.learning_objective: Interpret a grade I, stage I neoplasm as well-differentiated and localized.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Well-differentiated and localized"

questions.title: Signet ring carcinoma is a type of glandular carcinoma
questions.question: Signet ring carcinoma is a type of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous (non-glandular) epithelium and does not characteristically show the mucin-filled signet-ring morphology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transitional cell carcinoma arises from urothelial (transitional) epithelium, not the mucin-secreting glandular epithelium signet ring carcinoma derives from.
explanations.C: Correct. Signet ring carcinoma is a variant of glandular carcinoma (adenocarcinoma) in which tumour cells accumulate intracytoplasmic mucin that pushes the nucleus to the periphery, giving the cell its characteristic signet-ring appearance under the microscope. It classically occurs in the stomach and is a subtype of adenocarcinoma, a glandular malignancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma is a skin malignancy of basal keratinocytes, unrelated to the mucin-secreting glandular origin of signet ring carcinoma.

questions.subtopic: Signet ring carcinoma as a glandular carcinoma subtype
questions.learning_objective: Classify signet ring carcinoma as a subtype of glandular carcinoma.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Glandular carcinoma"

questions.title: The edges of a malignant ulcer are everted
questions.question: The edges of the malignant ulcer are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inverted edges are not the classic description of a malignant ulcer's margin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Undermined edges are classically associated with a tuberculous ulcer, not a malignant one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sharp, punched-out edge is more typical of a syphilitic (gummatous) ulcer.
explanations.D: Correct. The edge of a malignant ulcer is classically raised and everted (rolled outward). This reflects the unrestrained proliferative growth of the malignant epithelium at the ulcer margin, heaping up and turning outward over the ulcer base. It is a distinguishing clinical sign used to differentiate a malignant ulcer from benign or infective ulcer types with their own characteristic edge patterns (undermined in tuberculous, sharp/punched-out in syphilitic, sloping in a healing/traumatic ulcer).

questions.subtopic: Malignant ulcer edge -- raised and everted
questions.learning_objective: State that the edge of a malignant ulcer is raised and everted.

questions.title: Stroma separating individual cells distinguishes sarcoma from carcinoma
questions.question: The most important histologic feature that differentiates sarcoma from carcinoma is

options.D: Criteria of malignancy are more prominent

explanations.A: Incorrect. The degree of necrosis is not the specific histological feature used to distinguish sarcoma from carcinoma; both can show necrosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Sarcoma cells, arising from mesenchymal tissue, are typically dispersed as individual cells within an abundant connective-tissue stroma that separates them from one another. Carcinoma cells, arising from epithelium, instead grow cohesively in nests, sheets, glands or masses held together by cell junctions, with the stroma forming a supporting framework around groups of cells rather than separating individual tumour cells. This stromal relationship to individual cells is the key histological feature distinguishing the two.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Degree of vascularity varies by tumour type and grade in both sarcomas and carcinomas; it is not the defining histological distinguishing feature between the two categories.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both sarcomas and carcinomas show the general cytological criteria of malignancy (pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, mitoses); this does not distinguish one category from the other.

questions.learning_objective: State that stroma separating individual cells is the key histologic feature distinguishing sarcoma from carcinoma.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Stroma separates individual cells"
